Operator theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Algebra Linear algebra
OurBigBook.com Words: 17k Articles: 267
Linear operator theory studies linear maps, their spectra, invariant subspaces, and normal forms such as Jordan normal form. In a finite-dimensional vector space, eigenvalues identify parameters for which a shifted linear operator cannot be inverted. In an infinite-dimensional vector space, inversion can fail even without an eigenvector. The spectrum of a bounded operator captures this larger obstruction and connects linear algebra with the approximation questions of functional analysis.

Annihilating polynomial (p(A)=0)

Words: 140 Articles: 1
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
An annihilating polynomial of a linear operator is a nonzero polynomial p for which the displayed operator is zero. The minimal polynomial is its unique monic annihilating polynomial of least degree and divides every other annihilating polynomial. For a diagonalizable operator with distinct eigenvalues λ1​,…,λs​, the product ∏j​(t−λj​) annihilates it. For an individual vector it suffices to annihilate the eigenvalues contributing to that vector; this gives exact finite-step termination bounds for a Krylov subspace method.

Eigenspace decomposition from a square-free annihilating polynomial (∏j​(T−μj​I)=0⟹V=⨁j​ker(T−μj​I))

Words: 72
Annihilating polynomial OurBigBook.com
For distinct scalars μj​, the Lagrange interpolation polynomials ℓj​(t)=∏k=j​(t−μk​)/(μj​−μk​) sum to one. Their values at T have images in the respective eigenspaces, since (t−μj​)ℓj​ is a multiple of the annihilating polynomial. Hence every vector is the sum of its ℓj​(T) images. On the ith eigenspace, ℓj​(T) is multiplication by δij​, which proves directness. This gives the decomposition without invoking the primary decomposition theorem. Under this decomposition a linear operator commutes with T exactly when it preserves every eigenspace.

Differentiation operator (Df=f′)

Words: 62
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
The differentiation operator sends a differentiable function to its derivative; its domain and the norms must be specified. On C1([−1,1]) with values in C([−1,1]), using the supremum norm on both, it is an unbounded linear operator: fn​(x)=sin(nx) satisfies ∥fn​∥∞​≤1 and ∥Dfn​∥∞​=n. Its graph norm is ∥f∥∞​+∥f′∥∞​, which is complete. Indeed, the kernel consists of constants and is complete, while Sg(x)=∫0x​g(t)dt is a bounded right inverse by the fundamental theorem of calculus; apply completeness of a graph norm from a bounded right inverse.

Operator exponential (eA)

Words: 193 Articles: 2
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
For a bounded linear operator, the series eA=∑n=0∞​An/n! converges in operator norm. For an unbounded self-adjoint operator H, the spectral theorem instead defines the bounded unitary operator e−iHt/ℏ by applying the scalar function e−iEt/ℏ to its projection-valued measure. This yields unitary time evolution without assuming that every vector lies in the domain of every power of H. In finite dimensions it is the matrix exponential.

Exponential of a bounded skew-adjoint operator is unitary (T∗=−T⟹(eT)∗=(eT)−1=e−T)

Words: 73
Operator exponential OurBigBook.com
For a bounded skew-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space, the operator exponential converges in norm because its term norms are bounded by ∥T∥n/n!. Continuity of the adjoint operator gives (eT)∗=eT∗=e−T. Absolute convergence permits the Cauchy product of eT and e−T: its degree-n coefficient is Tn∑j=0n​(−1)j/[j!(n−j)!], zero for n>0 and the identity for n=0. Both multiplication orders therefore give the identity, proving unitarity. The boundedness hypothesis makes this elementary power-series proof valid without domain issues for unbounded generators.

Commutator of an operator with an exponential ([A,e−βB])

Words: 65
Operator exponential OurBigBook.com
For bounded linear operators, define C(β)=[A,e−βB]. The product rule gives C′+BC=[B,A]e−βB and C(0)=0. Multiplying by the integrating factor eβB yields
[A,e−βB]=e−βB∫0β​eλB[B,A]e−λBdλ.
(1)
The identity is useful when the two linear operators do not commute: it preserves their order rather than incorrectly differentiating an operator exponential as if all its factors were scalars. For unbounded linear operators, the products and differentiations need a common justified operator domain.

Polar decomposition (A=U∣A∣)

Words: 57
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
For a bounded operator A on a Hilbert space, set ∣A∣=(A∗A)1/2. There is a unique partial isometry U, zero on kerA, satisfying A=U∣A∣; on the range of ∣A∣, define U(∣A∣x)=Ax and extend by continuity. This is well-defined and isometric because ∥Ax∥2=⟨A∗Ax,x⟩=∥∣A∣x∥2. For an invertible square matrix, U is unitary.

Shift operator

Words: 241 Articles: 5
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
A shift operator translates the components of a function or sequence by a fixed displacement. Bilateral shifts act on doubly infinite sequences; the unilateral shift operator acts on a one-sided sequence space and has distinct forward and backward versions.

Unilateral shift operator

Words: 205 Articles: 4
Shift operator OurBigBook.com
The unilateral shifts on sequences move every component one place left or right. Their spectra illustrate behavior absent in finite dimensions.

Factorial weighted right shift (Tej​=ej+1​/j)

Words: 59
Unilateral shift operator OurBigBook.com
On the absolutely summable sequence space, this weighted shift has Tmej​=ej+m​/[j(j+1)⋯(j+m−1)], so ∥Tm∥=1/m!. The spectral radius formula gives radius zero. Its spectrum is exactly {0} because it is not onto, while it has no eigenvalues: zero is excluded by injectivity, and any nonzero eigenvalue equation forces all coordinates to vanish starting at the first. Thus it is a nonzero quasinilpotent element of the operator algebra.

Norm stability of noninvertibility for the unilateral right shift (∥A∥<1⟹R+A noninvertible)

Words: 51
Unilateral shift operator OurBigBook.com
On ℓ1​, the unilateral shift operator R and left shift operator L satisfy LR=I and ∥L∥=1, while L has nontrivial kernel. If ∥A∥<1, the Neumann series makes L(R+A)=I+LA invertible. Were R+A invertible, this identity would express L as a product of invertible operators, a contradiction. Thus the open unit ball about R contains no invertible operator.

Left shift operator (L(f1​,f2​,…)=(f2​,f3​,…))

Words: 37
Unilateral shift operator OurBigBook.com
On the Hilbert space ℓ2(N), the left shift deletes the first coordinate. It is the adjoint operator of the unilateral shift operator S. The identities LS=I and SLf=f−f1​e1​ show that it is also the Moore–Penrose inverse of an operator for S; both maps have operator norm one.

Wandering-vector characterization of a unilateral shift

Words: 37
Unilateral shift operator OurBigBook.com
An operator T is a unilateral shift exactly when it is an isometry, (ImT)⊥ is one-dimensional, and ⋂n≥1​Im(Tn)={0}. A unit vector e1​ in the first orthogonal complement is wandering, and en​=Tn−1e1​ is a complete orthonormal basis.

Solvability condition

Words: 79
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
A solvability condition is a compatibility requirement on data for an equation to admit a solution in a specified function space or with specified boundary behavior. For a bounded linear operator between Hilbert spaces, the equation Lu=f requires f to be orthogonal to the kernel of the adjoint. A closed range makes that requirement sufficient; the Fredholm alternative for a compact operator applies this principle to I−K with compact K. in an asymptotic inner problem, exclusion of a growing homogeneous mode can impose an analogous weighted-integral condition.

Spectrum (functional analysis, σ(T))

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
The spectrum of a linear operator consists of the scalars λ for which A−λI is not invertible. In finite dimensions it is the set of eigenvalues.

Spectrum of a nontrivial bounded projection (P2=P,P=0,I⟹σ(P)={0,1})

Words: 53
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
Let P be a bounded linear operator on a complex Banach space with P2=P, P=0 and P=I. Its image of a linear map and kernel contain nonzero vectors, giving eigenvalues one and zero. For λ∈/{0,1},
(λI−P)−1=λ−1(I−P)+(λ−1)−1P.
(2)
Direct multiplication proves the formula, so the spectrum is exactly {0,1} and its spectral radius is one. Since Pj=P and ∥P∥≥1, the spectral radius formula is explicit: infj≥1​∥Pj∥1/j=limj→∞​∥P∥1/j=1.

Point spectrum (σp​(T))

Words: 75
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
For a bounded linear operator T:X→X on a complex Banach space, the point spectrum is precisely its set of eigenvalues:
σp​(T)={λ∈C:ker(T−λI)={0}}.
(3)
Here I is the identity operator. Thus membership requires an actual nonzero eigenvector, whereas the spectrum of a bounded operator only requires failure of a bounded inverse. Every eigenvalue belongs to the spectrum, but the inclusion can be strict. The multiplication operator discussed below has an entire interval in its spectrum and empty point spectrum.[ref]

Approximate eigenvalue (λ∈σap​(T))

Words: 56 Articles: 1
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
An approximate eigenvalue of a bounded operator T is a scalar λ admitting unit vectors xn​ with ∥(T−λI)xn​∥→0. Every approximate eigenvalue belongs to the spectrum; for a normal operator, all spectral points are approximate eigenvalues.

Approximate eigenvector (∥un​∥=1,∥(A−λ)un​∥→0)

Words: 20
Approximate eigenvalue OurBigBook.com
The unit vectors realizing an approximate eigenvalue are approximate eigenvectors: their residual tends to zero, although they need not converge to any genuine eigenvector.

Residual spectrum (σr​(T))

Words: 45
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
In the disjoint convention for a bounded linear operator T, the residual spectrum consists of λ for which T−λI is injective but has nondense range. Together with the point spectrum and continuous spectrum it partitions the spectrum of a bounded operator. Some conventions also include noninjective operators with nondense range, so the convention must be stated.

Continuous spectrum

Words: 43
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
For a self-adjoint operator T, a real number λ lies in the continuous spectrum when T−λI is injective with dense range but is not surjective. Such spectral values need not be eigenvalues of normalizable states. The free-particle Hamiltonian on the real line has a continuous energy spectrum.

Spectrum of a bounded operator (σ(T)=C∖ρ(T))

Words: 751
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
Let X={0} be a Banach space over the complex numbers, and let T:X→X be a bounded linear operator defined on all of X. Its spectrum consists of those λ∈C for which T−λI has no everywhere-defined bounded inverse. Its complement is the resolvent set of an operator ρ(T). By the bounded inverse theorem, a bijective T−λI automatically has a bounded inverse. The spectrum is a nonempty compact subset of the complex plane, with
σ(T)⊆{λ∈C:∣λ∣≤∥T∥}.
(4)
The bound uses the operator norm, and nonemptiness uses the complex field.[ref] For a real linear operator, complex spectral values are understood by extending it to a complex vector space; restricting λ to the real field can give an empty set.
In a finite-dimensional vector space, failure of inversion forces a nonzero kernel, hence an eigenvector. An infinite-dimensional vector space allows an injective shifted linear operator that cannot solve every equation (T−λI)u=g. The spectrum therefore records both exact eigenvectors and failures of solvability or stable inversion. Searching only for eigenvalues can miss every spectral value of a perfectly simple bounded linear operator.
Consider the multiplication operator M on the complex L2 space L2([0,1],dx), with Lebesgue measure:
(Mf)(x)=xf(x),∥f∥22​=∫01​∣f(x)∣2dx.
(5)
Its operator norm is one. The inequality ∥Mf∥2​≤∥f∥2​ gives the upper bound; unit vectors concentrated near x=1 approach it. The result is
σ(M)=[0,1],σp​(M)=∅.
(6)
This is the interval example of the general connection between multiplication operators and the essential range of their multiplier.[ref] Indeed, an eigenfunction would satisfy (x−λ)f(x)=0 almost everywhere. It vanishes except possibly on the singleton {λ}, a null set; such a function is the zero vector in L2 space. Concentrating at one point cannot produce a nonzero L2 function.
For λ∈/[0,1], the inverse is completely explicit:
((M−λI)−1g)(x)=x−λg(x)​,∥(M−λI)−1∥=dist(λ,[0,1])1​.
(7)
The distance to a set is positive, so the inverse multiplier is bounded. Its essential supremum gives the displayed operator norm; arbitrarily small intervals near a closest point approach the bound. Our resolvent of an operator uses (λI−M)−1, the negative of this inverse, with the same operator norm. For λ=−1/4, 5/4, and 1/2+i/10, the inverse norms are respectively 4, 4, and 10. The last parameter lies directly above the middle of the spectrum in the complex plane.
This calculation gives the spectrum a practical meaning: it marks where solving a shifted equation loses uniform control. At λ=1/2+iη, the largest amplification of an input error is 1/∣η∣. Changing η from 0.1 to 0.01 increases that factor from ten to one hundred. The equation remains uniquely solvable for each nonzero η, but its sensitivity grows as the parameter approaches the spectrum.
To see directly why every λ∈[0,1] belongs to the spectrum, choose 0<ε<1 and define a clipped interval and a normalized indicator function:
a=max(0,λ−ε),b=min(1,λ+ε),ℓ=b−a,uλ,ε​(x)=ℓ−1/21[a,b]​(x).
(8)
Its L2 norm is exactly one, including at both endpoints. On its support, ∣x−λ∣≤ε, giving
∥(M−λI)uλ,ε​∥22​=3ℓ(b−λ)3−(a−λ)3​≤ε2.
(9)
Thus any choice εn​→0 produces approximate eigenvectors. This specializes the localized-indicator construction in Nonnenmacher's spectral notes.[ref] A hypothetical bounded inverse B would imply 1=∥uλ,ε​∥2​≤∥B∥ε, impossible for arbitrarily small ε.
For an interior point with ε≤min(λ,1−λ), ℓ=2ε and the residual is exactly ε/3​. At λ=0 or 1, ℓ=ε and the same residual formula holds, but the amplitude is ε−1/2 rather than (2ε)−1/2. At λ=1/2, taking ε=0.2,0.1,0.05 gives amplitudes approximately 1.5811,2.2361,3.1623 and residuals 0.11547,0.057735,0.028868. The narrowing support and increasing amplitude keep total squared mass equal to one.
For every λ∈[0,1], the continuous spectrum description is also concrete. Any L2 function g can be approximated in L2 norm by its truncations to ∣x−λ∣≥δ. Each truncation lies in the range of M−λI, since division there is bounded. The range is therefore dense. However, the constant function g=1 has no L2 function preimage: 1/(x−λ) is not square-integrable, including at the endpoints.
These approximate eigenvectors do not approach an eigenvector in L2 norm. Any possible limit would have L2 norm one and satisfy (M−λI)u=0 by continuity, contradicting the empty point spectrum. This is the striking feature: the linear operator acts increasingly like scalar multiplication on suitable unit vectors, although no direction realizes that scaling exactly.
A complementary example is the diagonal operator on sequence space (Dx)n​=xn​/n on complex l2 sequence space, with n=1,2,…. The coordinate unit vectors satisfy Den​=(1/n)en​, so
σp​(D)={1/n:n≥1},σ(D)={0}∪{1/n:n≥1}.
(10)
Zero is not an eigenvalue, since Dx=0 forces every coordinate to vanish. Nevertheless ∥Den​∥=1/n→0: these are approximate eigenvectors at zero. More concretely, g=(1/n)n≥1​ belongs to l2 sequence space, but Dx=g would require xn​=1 for all n, which does not. Outside the displayed closed set, division by 1/n−λ is uniformly bounded, proving that no further spectral values occur. Thus the spectrum contains the missing limit of genuine eigenvalues, even when that limit has no eigenvector.

Eigenvalue (λ)

Words: 3k Articles: 51
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
A scalar λ is an eigenvalue of a linear operator A:V→V when
Av=λv
(54)
for some nonzero vector v, called an eigenvector. The scalar must belong to the field over which V is a vector space. Geometrically, a real eigenvalue tells us what A does along a special line: every vector on that line is multiplied by the same number. The eigenvector gives the line and the eigenvalue gives its scaling.
For a real eigenvalue, λ>0 preserves the orientation along the line, λ<0 reverses it, and λ=0 collapses the line to zero. The length is multiplied by the modulus ∣λ∣, so ∣λ∣>1 stretches and 0<∣λ∣<1 contracts. For example, the diagonal matrix diag(2,−1/2,0) doubles one coordinate direction, reverses and halves another, and annihilates the third. Its eigenvalues are 2,−1/2,0; the last direction lies in its kernel.
For a finite square matrix, the eigenvalues are the roots of a polynomial pA​, its characteristic polynomial:
pA​(λ)=det(λI−A)=0.
(55)
Here I is the identity matrix. The reason is that Av=λv means (A−λI)v=0 with v=0: the shifted matrix must have a nontrivial kernel, equivalently a zero determinant. The worked symmetric matrix example in eigenvector shows both stages: find the eigenvalues, then find their eigenspaces.
Eigenvalues are especially useful for repeated application of a linear map. If Av=λv, then
Anv=λnv(n≥0).
(56)
One multiplication proves the next step, so a matrix power becomes an ordinary power on each eigenvector. This explains growth, decay, and alternating signs along these directions. Gilbert Strang develops this connection, and its extension to the matrix exponential, in his lecture "Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors" (MIT 18.065, 2018).[ref]
A documented historical connection is C. G. J. Jacobi's "Über ein leichtes Verfahren die in der Theorie der Säcularstörungen vorkommenden Gleichungen numerisch aufzulösen" (1846, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 30, pp. 51–94). Its opening discusses symmetric matrices arising from small oscillations, with a common unknown subtracted from every diagonal entry. In modern notation this is (A−λI)v=0; Jacobi seeks the parameter and the ratios of the components of v. This is evidence of an early physical and computational setting for the eigenvalue problem, without assigning its discovery to a single person.[ref][ref]

A nonzero vector v is an eigenvector of a linear operator A when Av=λv for some eigenvalue λ. For a real vector space and λ=0, the line through v is preserved: the image can point forward or backward, but cannot turn away from that line. When λ=0, the image is zero and has no direction. The zero vector is excluded because it satisfies the equation for every scalar and identifies no special direction.
Every nonzero scalar multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector for the same eigenvalue, since A(cv)=cAv=λ(cv). Thus there is usually no preferred length or sign; choosing a unit vector is a convenient normalization. Eigenvectors for a fixed eigenvalue, together with zero, form its eigenspace.

This change of basis reveals a linear map as independent one-dimensional scalings. The matrix may look coupled in the original coordinates, but each coordinate in the eigenbasis evolves on its own.
For the symmetric matrix A=(21​12​) computed in eigenvector, take
P=(11​1−1​),P−1=21​(11​1−1​),D=(30​01​).
(71)
Then AP=PD, hence P−1AP=D. The orthonormal basis version is Q=P/2​, an orthogonal matrix satisfying QTAQ=D. Every real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis by the spectral theorem; a general diagonalizable matrix need not have orthogonal eigenvectors.
The immediate payoff is repeated application: adjacent factors P−1P cancel, giving An=PDnP−1. In this example,
An=21​(3n+13n−1​3n−13n+1​),An(10​)=21​(3n(11​)+(1−1​)).
(72)
The component in E3​ grows while the component in E1​ stays fixed. After division by its Euclidean norm, this particular sequence approaches (1,1)T/2​. This is the mechanism behind the power method; an initial vector entirely in E1​ would stay there and never find the dominant eigenvalue 3.
Two different obstructions deserve comparison. The planar rotation R in eigenvector is diagonalizable over C but not over R, because its eigenvalues are i and −i. By contrast, the shear mapping
S=(10​11​),(S−I)(xy​)=(y0​)
(73)
has only λ=1, of algebraic multiplicity two, and E1​=span{(1,0)T}, of geometric multiplicity one. There is no second independent eigenvector, even over C. This is a defective matrix, already a two-dimensional Jordan block. Its powers are
Sn=(10​n1​),Sn(01​)=(n1​).
(74)
Thus even though both eigenvalues are one, repeated application can produce growth. Eigenvalues alone miss the coupling recorded by a Jordan block. A repeated eigenvalue is harmless when it has enough independent eigenvectors, as I demonstrates. More generally, a matrix is diagonalizable exactly when its characteristic polynomial splits over the chosen field and every eigenvalue has equal geometric multiplicity and algebraic multiplicity. The proof outline is to join bases of the distinct eigenspaces; their direct sum fills the space exactly under these conditions.
A physical motivation is the separation of normal modes. Consider two equal masses m between three identical springs of stiffness k, with the outer ends fixed. By Hooke's law and Newton's second law, the displacement vector q=(q1​,q2​)T obeys
mq¨​=−kKq,K=(2−1​−12​).
(75)
The eigenvectors (1,1)T and (1,−1)T have eigenvalues 1 and 3: the masses move together in the first normal mode and oppositely in the second. Writing q=a(t)(1,1)T+b(t)(1,−1)T separates the coupled equations into two harmonic oscillators,
a¨+mk​a=0,b¨+m3k​b=0.
(76)
Their angular frequencies are k/m​ and 3k/m​; the eigenvalues give squared angular frequencies after multiplication by k/m. This is the beauty of diagonalization: finding the right directions turns interacting motions into independent patterns. For a physical treatment, see Yen-Jie Lee's "Coupled Oscillators, Normal Modes" (MIT 8.03SC, 2016), and the local article normal modes of two equal masses between three springs.[ref]

A splitting polynomial is square-free exactly when the characteristic of a field does not divide n, as follows by taking its derivative nXn−1 and checking common roots. is not a diagonalizable matrix over the rational numbers, since the quadratic factor has no rational root. More generally, diagonalizability is equivalent to the minimal polynomial splitting into distinct linear factors over the specified field.
For an integer matrix, reduction modulo a prime number is a different operation from extension of its coefficient field, and can merge eigenvalues. In the same example modulo 5, χA​(t)=(t−1)(t−3)2, while ker(A−3I) is spanned by (1,3,4)T. Thus the geometric multiplicity of 3 is one and its algebraic multiplicity is two, preventing diagonalizability even though all eigenvalues belong to the finite field.

This is the key step in simultaneous diagonalization of commuting linear maps.

The largest value is 3 along e+​; the smallest is 1 along e−​. A direction halfway between them has quotient 2. In the left panel, the color on the unit circle represents the quotient; in the right panel, the same values are plotted against the angle measured from e+​.
The Hermitian Rayleigh quotient range explains why this is useful: evaluating one trial vector gives an upper bound on the smallest eigenvalue and a lower bound on the largest one, without solving a characteristic polynomial. At an extreme eigenvector, a small angular error changes the quotient only quadratically. Near e+​ in this example, 3−RA​(q(θ))=2sin2θ=2θ2+O(θ4). This is the geometric reason for quadratic Rayleigh-quotient improvement for the power method and motivates the Rayleigh-Ritz method.
There is a concrete historical link with normal modes. In The Theory of Sound (1877), Volume I, Sections 88–89, Lord Rayleigh studies the period of a constrained trial vibration. He shows that the period has a stationary point at a normal mode and that a trial type bounds the longest natural period. These energy ratios are a mechanical setting for the modern Rayleigh quotient and generalized Rayleigh quotient; the book describes the result through vibration periods, rather than today's matrix notation.[ref]

Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions do this by setting η=0 at the ends; homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions do it through y′=0. More general self-adjoint boundary conditions can require a boundary contribution to the quadratic form.
For an eigenfunction, the weaker identity [pyy′]ab​=0 suffices to give λ=Λ[y] by integration by parts, but it does not by itself imply the condition on every variation. An explicit counterexample uses p=q=w=1 on [0,1] and y=cosπx+sinπx. This solves −y′′+y=(1+π2)y and has [yy′]01​=0. Define a nearby family

A Neumann boundary condition only at the lower endpoint does not remove the upper boundary term. Equality with k2 additionally requires ϕ(z2​)ϕ′(z2​)=0. With the lower condition, nonconstant oscillatory solutions satisfy this when their phase advance is an integer multiple of π/2; affine solutions must be constant, while nonzero hyperbolic-cosine solutions fail the condition. Hermitian Rayleigh quotient range ([λmin​,λmax​])

Words: 125
Rayleigh quotient OurBigBook.com
For a finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix A, the Rayleigh quotient has precisely the range [λmin​,λmax​], where the endpoints are its extreme eigenvalues. The finite-dimensional spectral theorem writes a nonzero vector as x=∑j​cj​ej​ in an orthonormal eigenbasis, giving
RA​(x)=∑j​λj​wj​,wj​=∑k​∣ck​∣2∣cj​∣2​,wj​≥0,∑j​wj​=1.
(92)
Thus the quotient is a convex combination of eigenvalues. The bounds follow immediately, and equality at either endpoint means that x lies in the corresponding extreme eigenspace, including any repeated eigenvalue. Every intermediate value occurs: for orthonormal extreme eigenvectors, x=1−t​emin​+t​emax​ gives RA​(x)=(1−t)λmin​+tλmax​ for 0≤t≤1. If all eigenvalues are equal, the quotient is constant.
The Hermitian hypothesis matters. The real matrix B=(10​41​) has only the eigenvalue 1, but (1,1)B(1,1)T/2=3. Its quotient is governed by the symmetric part of a matrix (B+BT)/2, not by a real orthonormal eigenbasis of B. A nonsymmetric matrix therefore need not obey the displayed eigenvalue bounds.

It vanishes exactly when Ax=RA​(x)x, so the stationary points are eigenvectors. Equivalently, the Lagrange multiplier condition for optimizing xTAx on the unit sphere is Ax=λx. The smallest and largest eigenvalues give the global extrema; other eigenvectors can be stationary without being extrema, as a direction mixing larger and smaller eigenvalues changes the quotient in opposite ways.

Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle

The extremal Rayleigh quotients of a self-adjoint operator are the extremal spectral values. In particular, a Hamiltonian with a discrete spectrum satisfies R[ψ]≥E0​, with equality precisely on its ground-state eigenspace. More generally, minimizing over states orthogonal to the first j eigenspaces gives an upper bound on Ej​.

Their cross terms vanish in both the L2 inner product and the Dirichlet energy form: each integrand is odd about the midpoint. Their separate Rayleigh quotients are R[s]=10 and R[a]=42. Thus every quotient on their two-dimensional span is a positive weighted average of ten and forty-two, so the minimum remains ten. Adding a direction with the wrong symmetry need not improve the ground-state estimate.
The symmetric quartic s2=r2(1−r)2 does add a useful direction. On the span of s,s2, the generalized eigenvalue problem has stiffness matrix K=(1/31/15​1/152/105​) and mass matrix M=(1/301/140​1/1401/630​). Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle OurBigBook.com

The Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle says that every admissible nonzero trial profile gives an upper bound on the bottom of the spectrum, and on the lowest eigenvalue when this bottom is attained by a fundamental diffusion mode. Finite weighted energy, rather than pointwise existence of a second derivative at the origin, is the relevant trial admissibility requirement.

Cyclic vector (V=span{v,Tv,T2v,…})

Words: 177 Articles: 2
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
For a linear operator T, a cyclic vector is a vector whose iterates span the entire vector space. In finite dimension d, the vectors v,Tv,…,Td−1v then form a basis: the first linear dependence makes the preceding span invariant under T, so later iterates cannot enlarge it. In topological settings one often requires the iterates to have dense span instead; that closure convention must be stated.

Cyclic operator has equal minimal and characteristic polynomials (mT​=cT​)

Words: 68
Cyclic vector OurBigBook.com
On a d-dimensional vector space, a cyclic vector v gives a basis v,Tv,…,Td−1v. Write Tdv=−∑j<d​cj​Tjv and set f(t)=td+∑j<d​cj​tj. Then f(T)v=0. Since polynomials in T commute with T, f(T) kills every basis vector, so f(T)=0. No nonzero polynomial of degree less than d can kill v, by linear independence. Hence the minimal polynomial is f. The matrix in this basis is C(f), and the characteristic polynomial of a companion matrix is f as well.

A cyclic subspace generated by x under a linear operator T is the span of its successive iterates x,Tx,T2x,…. In finite dimension it is already generated by the first n iterates. The first linear dependence expresses the next iterate in previous ones and proves invariance without using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

Operator theory OurBigBook.com

With column vectors it has ones on the subdiagonal and last column (−c0​,…,−cd−1​)T. For example, C(t2+ct+d)=(01​−d−c​). Transposing this matrix gives another common convention, so the subdiagonal convention should be specified when giving entries.

In tI−C(f), the cofactors of the last-column entries, from top to bottom, are 1,t,…,td−1. This follows by expanding their bidiagonal minors: the subdiagonal factors −1 cancel the cofactor signs. Laplace expansion along that column therefore gives c0​+c1​t+⋯+cd−2​td−2+(t+cd−1​)td−1=f(t). The degree-one case is the same identity for the one-by-one matrix (−c0​).

Rational canonical form

Words: 665 Articles: 8
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
The rational canonical form of a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field is a direct sum C(f1​)⊕⋯⊕C(fr​) of companion matrices, where the monic nonconstant invariant factors of a linear operator satisfy f1​∣⋯∣fr​. Their degrees sum to the dimension of the space. It exists over any field and classifies similar matrices, without requiring their eigenvalues to lie in that field. It comes from the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain, applied to the module in which the indeterminate acts as the given operator.

Nullity of a cyclic linear operator (dimkerα=1{d(0)=0}​)

Words: 97
Rational canonical form OurBigBook.com
For a nonzero finite-dimensional cyclic linear operator, identify its module with K[X]/(d), where d is the monic minimal polynomial. Its kernel consists of classes of h with d∣Xh. If d(0)=0, coprimality gives d∣h, so the kernel is zero. If d=Xe, it consists precisely of the multiples of e modulo Xe, a one-dimensional space. Thus the multiplicity of zero as a root of d does not increase the nullity. The same companion block reads off invertibility from the constant term and gives the characteristic and minimal polynomials directly, while explicitly listing eigenvalues may require factoring d.

Rational canonical form of an inverse (f(t)↦f∨(t)=tdf(1/t)/f(0))

Words: 110
Rational canonical form OurBigBook.com
Let an invertible matrix T have monic invariant factors of a linear operator fj​ of degrees dj​. Their constant coefficients are nonzero, since their product is the characteristic polynomial and detT=0. On a cyclic block, f(T)=0 implies T−df(T)=0, so f∨(T−1)=0, where f∨(t)=tdf(1/t)/f(0) is monic of degree d. The vector v remains cyclic for T−1: multiplying v,T−1v,…,T−(d−1)v by the invertible map Td−1 gives the reversed original cyclic basis. Thus this polynomial is the minimal polynomial of the inverse block.
Normalized reciprocation preserves divisibility because (fg)∨=f∨g∨ when both constant coefficients are nonzero. Consequently the rational canonical form of T−1 is the direct sum of the companion matrices C(fj∨​). The normalization by fj​(0) is essential to make each reciprocal polynomial monic.

Rational canonical form under an affine change (f(t)↦adegff((t−b)/a)(a=0))

Words: 120
Rational canonical form OurBigBook.com
Let U=aT+bI on a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space over a field, with a=0. An invariant block for T is also invariant for U. If v,Tv,…,Td−1v is its cyclic vector basis, then v,Uv,…,Ud−1v is another basis: the binomial theorem gives a triangular change-of-basis matrix with diagonal 1,a,…,ad−1. The monic polynomial g(t)=adf((t−b)/a) annihilates this block, and its degree is d, so it is the block's minimal polynomial. In the new cyclic basis the block is C(g).
The substitution preserves divisibility of the monic invariant factors of a linear operator. Apply it to every block to obtain the rational canonical form of U. If a=0, then U=bI is a scalar matrix instead: all invariant factors are t−b, one for each dimension. This exceptional case cannot be obtained by dividing by a.

Rational canonical form with irreducible minimal polynomial (mA​=f irreducible⟹A∼Cf⊕n/degf​)

Words: 69
Rational canonical form OurBigBook.com
Let A act on a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space over a field F, with minimal polynomial an irreducible polynomial f of polynomial degree d. The nonconstant invariant factors of a linear operator all divide f, so each equals f. Their degrees sum to the dimension of a vector space, giving d∣n and rational canonical form consisting of n/d copies of the companion matrix Cf​. Equivalently, make the vector space a module over the field F[X]/(f) by letting X act as A; a basis over this field gives the same block decomposition.

Suppose the rational canonical form of T is C(f1​)⊕⋯⊕C(fr​), with monic nonconstant invariant factors of a linear operator satisfying f1​∣⋯∣fr​. Each block has minimal polynomial and characteristic polynomial fj​, because a cyclic operator has equal minimal and characteristic polynomials. The determinant of a block diagonal matrix is the product of block determinants, giving cT​=∏j​fj​. A polynomial kills the direct sum exactly when it kills each block, equivalently when every fj​ divides it. Thus mT​ is their least common multiple, which the divisibility chain reduces to fr​. On the zero vector space both polynomials are conventionally one.
